content: BALB/c is an albino strain of laboratory mouse that has served as the progenitor for numerous commonly used substrains. These mice, now over 200 generations removed from their origin in New York in 1920, are distributed globally and are among the most widely utilized inbred strains in animal experimentation. The founding animals of the BALB/c strain were acquired by Halsey J. Bagg of Memorial Hospital, New York, from a mouse dealer in Ohio in 1913. Starting in 1920, the descendants of this original colony were systematically inbred through sibling-to-sibling matings for 26 generations over a span of 15 years. This process was carried out by C.C.J. Muller at the University of Texas. By 1935, the mice were in the possession of Muller’s student, George Davis Snell, who transferred them to The Jackson Laboratory. This stock became the foundation for all BALB/c substrains currently in use worldwide. Snell also provided some of these animals to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for maintenance. In 1961, D.W. Bailey used some of the NIH-maintained stock to develop a substrain at the University of California, San Francisco. By 1974, these animals, now 136 generations removed from the original breeding pair, were returned to The Jackson Laboratory and designated as BALB/cByJ. On November 16, 2005, The Jackson Laboratory reported that this substrain had reached its 235th generation. In 1938 or 1939, Snell also provided J. Paul Scott with some BALB/c breeding stock. When a fire destroyed the main buildings of The Jackson Laboratory in 1947, all of Snell’s original breeding stock perished. However, Scott’s mice, housed in a separate building, survived. Scott donated stock back to repopulate the colony, starting at generation 41. The descendants of these mice are now referred to as BALB/cJ, which, as of December 14, 2006, were 221 generations removed from the founding stock. Other less commonly used substrains, such as BALB/cWt, are maintained at The Jackson Laboratory, while the BALB/cN substrain is maintained by the NIH. BALB/c mice are particularly valuable for research in oncology and immunology. According to Michael Festing’s Inbred Strains of Mice, BALB/c substrains are especially well-known for their ability to produce plasmacytomas when injected with mineral oil, a critical process for the production of monoclonal antibodies. These mice are also characterized by a low incidence of mammary tumors but are prone to developing other types of cancers later in life, most commonly reticular neoplasms, lung tumors, and renal tumors. Most substrains exhibit a long reproductive lifespan and are noted for their high levels of anxiety. Additionally, they are relatively resistant to diet-induced atherosclerosis, making them a useful model for cardiovascular research. There are notable differences between various BALB/c substrains, which are believed to arise from mutations rather than genetic contamination. For instance, male BALB/c mice are aggressive and will fight other males if housed together. However, the BALB/Lac substrain is significantly more docile. The BALB/cWt substrain is also unique in that 3% of its progeny exhibit true hermaphroditism.
